Rank scan skipped: a map ranking scan went over the client's monthly credit limit. Competitor suggestions ready, Client updated their setup and Setup waiting on you: where a client's setup stands. An account manager who covers only some clients gets these only for those clients. Slack and Teams messages are set up under Agency settings, not here.

Each row has two switches. In-app puts the notice in your Inbox; Email sends it to the address on this list. Both start on. A switch saves the moment you change it, and only affects new notices. With both on, you get the same notice both ways.

Instant alerts: one change that matters, sent when it is ready. Alert digest: alerts held back for an evening roundup. Weekly brief: your brief for the week. Quarterly report: the report written after each quarter. A few messages, such as an invitation to join, are needed for your account and have no switch.

Fill in both a start and an end to turn quiet hours on; clear one of them and save to turn them off. A window can run overnight, such as 21:00 to 07:00. Emails that would arrive inside it are held and sent when it ends. In-app notices still arrive at once.
There is one card for each place you receive notices from, titled with its name. Switches, time zone and quiet hours are saved separately for each card.
The clock your quiet hours follow. Left on Business time zone, they follow US Central time (America/Chicago). Pick a zone if you want your own local time.
The clock your quiet hours follow. Left on Business time zone, they follow the time zone saved for your business. Pick a zone if you want your own local time.

Alerts for clients set to "I review alerts first". Approve one to send it to the client, or dismiss it with a reason. Unreviewed alerts expire after 7 days. The list shows the oldest 200; filter by client to see more.
Alerts appear here for clients set to "I review alerts first" when a change scores at their alert level. Clients in other alert modes get theirs without a check.

A client gets at most 3 instant alerts a day. When you approve one past that limit, it goes in the client's 17:00 digest (client time) instead of being sent at once. Held alerts can only be dismissed.
How much the change matters to the client, from 0 to 100. A change becomes an alert at the client's alert level, which is 70 unless you changed it under Alert rules.
{assistant} writes each alert and checks its wording against the evidence. When it can't verify the wording, the alert uses the plain evidence summary instead. It is safe to send, just less polished.
{assistant} drafts each client's brief on Thursday night, in the client's time zone. Review and approve it for Monday 07:00. Clients set to auto-send get untouched briefs then without your approval.
Check each item against its evidence, edit or remove what you do not want, then approve. The client sees only the items that remain.

Approving schedules the brief for Monday 07:00 in the client's time zone, and its items become the client's recommendations. A starting-point brief is sent straight away. Send now approves it if needed and sends it to the client's recipients at once. The Monday auto-send switch is for clients whose untouched briefs you trust.

How sure the draft is about an item, as a percentage. At 85% and above it reads "High confidence" and gets an amber edge; below that it reads "Confidence". It is a prompt to look closer, not a verdict.
Every sentence left in the brief was checked against saved evidence. When the check removed a sentence or an item because it could not prove it, the page says how many.
Useful and Not useful record your feedback on one item. You can rate an item at any time, even after the brief is sent.
The upsell tag marks an item that points to a service you could sell. Only you see it: it is never part of the brief the client reads.
Each client's brief appears here after {assistant} drafts it on Thursday night. Open it to check every item against its evidence, then approve it.
Nothing below needs a decision from you right now.
Nothing is waiting for your review

The count shows items still in the brief and items removed from it (by the fact-check or by you). Edited means someone changed the draft. Auto-send means the client gets an untouched brief on Monday 07:00 without approval. Quiet week means no significant competitor moves.

Ready for review: drafted and waiting for you. Approved: it goes out Monday 07:00. Sent: delivered to the client. Drafting: still being written. Failed — retrying: the draft failed and will run again.
Seven short screens to add a client: who they are, their Google listing, what they do and where, their competitors, the owner invite, billing and a final check.

The kind of business, such as HVAC and plumbing or dental. It sets the topics, plays and alert levels the client starts with, and the services you can pick. If none fits, create a new business type from the listing; it is reviewed later and may be merged into an existing one.
Choose "Can't find it? Continue without a listing". We place the business from the address you entered, or ask for a City or ZIP on the next screen. You can link a Google listing later in Settings.

We need the business name and the owner contact: their name, phone and email. The address is optional. The preview shows the top of the brief they will receive. The contact is suggested later as the person to invite.

The screens are: Client details, Find the business, What they do and where, Pick who to watch, Invite the owner, Set up billing and All set. The client is created at the end of the second screen. Save and exit keeps your progress, and the setup reopens where you left off.
Businesses that asked for a competitor snapshot, through your intake link or assigned to you from the platform. Accept one to set it up as a prospect and invite the contact.
Leads you accept appear here with a link to their setup.
Share your intake link to start getting them. New requests appear here once the contact confirms their email.

Accept and invite creates the business as a prospect, starts its setup and emails the contact an invitation as the client owner. Pick the business type first. Decline closes the lead; for a lead from your link you can tick "Let them know" to tell them. A declined lead from the platform goes back to the pool and the contact is not emailed.
A short preview of how the business shows locally. While it is still being built the card says so, and some leads have none.
"From your website" means the contact used your intake link. "From the platform" means the lead was assigned to you from the shared lead pool.
New holds leads whose contact has confirmed their email and that you have not decided on. Accepted and Declined hold the ones you decided on. The number is how many leads are in each tab.
Every client at a glance, and what needs you today. Clients with an alert to check or a brief to approve come first, then the highest pressure.
Add a client by searching for its business. A short setup then finds its competitors, invites the owner and sets up billing, and its first brief follows.
The clients you are assigned to show here. Ask an agency admin to add a client or to give you access to one.

Alerts counts the alerts held for your check (clients set to "I review alerts first"); the line under it is how many were sent to that client in the last 7 days. Brief shows the newest brief that needs review. Open either one from the table.

This month's credits used by the client, as a share of its monthly credit limit. From 80% it reads Near limit and at 100% Limit reached; nothing changes at that point. Well past the limit, AI and monitoring work for the client pauses until next month and it reads Paused.

Agency admins see a getting-started card with what is still open: add your first client, add a payment method while you are on the trial, and invite your team or add your logo and colours if you skipped those. It goes away when nothing is left or when you dismiss it.
Recommendations for the client that are still To do or In progress. Click the number to open them.

How much the client's busiest competitor has been doing lately, from 0 to 100: its changes from the last 30 days that made the brief or an alert, plus its open moves. The label reads High pressure (70 and above), Medium pressure (40 to 69), Low pressure (1 to 39) or Quiet (0). The line under it names that competitor and the main reasons.

Shows while a client's setup is still open: how many setup steps are finished out of the total. "Waiting on" and a name means you asked the owner to pick the competitors and they haven't yet. Click it to open the setup.
Businesses you're pitching. A snapshot shows how they stack up locally. Nothing is monitored until you convert them.
Find their competitors, run a one-off snapshot, and show the landscape. Nothing is monitored until you convert them.

Converting turns the prospect into an active client: weekly monitoring, alerts and briefs start, and it counts as a client on your plan. If your plan is at its client limit, or your billing needs attention, the page says so and an agency admin can upgrade. If the setup's last step is still open, it reopens at billing.

A Google profile and ads table, and how the business and its competitors show on Google Maps across a 3 by 3 grid of the service area. It is built from Google Business Profile, ad-library and Google Maps data with no AI-written text, and usually takes a few minutes.

Profile, Competitors, Snapshot, Convert. The snapshot needs at least one keyword, a service area and at least one competitor; the page lists what is missing. You can run it again later for a fresh look.
Add a business you're pitching, pick its competitors and run a snapshot to show how it compares locally. Convert it to a client when it signs.
Ask an agency admin to add a prospect. Prospects you are assigned to show here.
Six short screens to add a business you are pitching: who they are, their Google listing, what they do and where, their competitors, the owner invite and a final check.
The kind of business, such as HVAC and plumbing or dental. It sets which services you can pick and what the competitor search looks for.
A prospect uses the same screens as a client. We need the business name and a contact: their name, phone and email. The contact is suggested later as the person to invite.

The screens are the same as for a client, without billing: Client details, Find the business, What they do and where, Pick who to watch, Invite the owner and All set. Then open the prospect and run a snapshot.
A business you are pitching. A prospect has no weekly monitoring, alerts or briefs: you pick its competitors and run a one-off snapshot, then convert it to a client when it signs.

A check mark means the prospect has at least one keyword, a service area and at least one competitor, which is what a snapshot needs. "Needs setup" means one of them is missing; open the prospect to see which.
Shows the latest snapshot for the prospect: running while it is being built, ready when you can open the landscape, failed if it did not finish (run it again). A dash means none has been run.
Connect Claude, ChatGPT or another AI assistant to every client you can access. When it matters, it asks which client you mean.
Paste the connector URL into Claude or ChatGPT and sign in. The app then shows up here.
Create one when a tool such as Claude Code needs access. Assistants you connect by signing in, like Claude or ChatGPT, do not need a token.

Apps that were connected by signing in, rather than with a token. Each shows its access level and which workspace it can reach. Disconnect removes its access straight away, and the app has to ask again next time. Admins see everyone's tokens and apps in the agency; account managers see their own.

Paste the connector URL into your AI assistant, then sign in and choose this workspace. Claude and ChatGPT add it from their Connectors settings. For Claude Code, create a token first and run the command shown; its server name is made from your agency name.

Read only lets an assistant look things up. Read and feedback also lets it record feedback, such as changing a recommendation's status. Read, feedback and manage also lets it make changes that need manage permission, such as setting a client's alert levels. A token or connected app never gets more than your own role allows.

A token is a password for tools that cannot sign in, such as Claude Code or a script. It acts as you, with the access level you choose. It is shown once when you create it, so copy it straight away. Revoke it at any time and anything using it stops working.
Your plan and how many clients it covers, your next invoice, and how your own clients pay you.
Invoices appear here after the first payment, each with a link to open it.

Connect your own Stripe account to bill your clients for monitoring: payments go straight to you, not through your plan. Once connected, set the default monthly price and setup fee, and optionally pause unpaid clients after a number of days (1 to 90). A new price applies to new sign-ups; existing subscriptions are unchanged. A paused client is no longer monitored and stops counting toward your plan.
If you have a discount code, enter it and choose Redeem code. The discount then shows on the plan card and in the amount of your next invoice.
The amount and date of your next invoice: the plan price plus any extra clients, less a discount if you redeemed a code. Recent invoices lists past payments, each with a link to open the invoice.

The plan card shows your monthly price, how many clients the plan includes and the price of each extra client. Read the figures there: plans can be priced differently. A client counts toward the included number when it is active and not paused; prospects and paused clients do not count, and the Clients line shows the count. Going over the included number bills each extra client at the price on the card (an increase is prorated at once, a decrease applies at the next renewal). If you signed up yourself, a trial allows 1 active client until you add a payment method.

Pilot and Free trial are free periods; the end date is shown. Active: paid up. Payment overdue: a payment failed or the trial ended without a card. Everything still works, but you cannot add active clients, and service pauses 7 days after it went overdue (the page shows the date). Read-only: history stays viewable, but monitoring, briefs, alerts and the assistant stop. Suspended follows 30 days later: only this page works, and your data is kept. Cancelled: access ends on the date shown. A successful payment makes the account Active again at once.
Make the app and your emails look like your agency. Set the name, logo and colours your clients see, who emails come from, and what the assistant is called.
What your clients call the Ask assistant, up to 30 characters. Leave it blank to use the default name shown in the box.
Primary and secondary colour take a six-digit hex code such as #47A8E7. A value that is not a valid code falls back to the default. The amber accent is fixed and can't be changed.
The name your clients see in the app, on your intake page and in emails. Leave it blank and they see your agency's registered name. Up to 80 characters.

Paste an https link to your logo, or upload a PNG, JPEG, WebP or SVG up to 512 KB; an upload is resized to fit 512 by 512 pixels and saved as a PNG. With no logo, your display name is shown as text instead.

The from-name is the name on the emails your clients receive. If you leave it blank it is your display name. The sign-off is a line added at the end of those emails, up to 300 characters. The sending address is not set on this page.
A public page where businesses ask for a free competitor snapshot. New requests appear under Leads.
What visitors see on your intake page. Nothing here can be submitted.
New this month counts leads from this link whose contact confirmed their email since the start of the month (UTC). Accepted counts every lead from this link that you have accepted.

The public page for your agency, at the address shown. Visitors search for their business and ask for a free competitor snapshot; once they confirm their email you decide under Leads. Copy link gives you the address, and Copy button HTML gives a ready-made button for your website in your primary colour.

The last part of your address: 3 to 40 lowercase letters, digits or hyphens. If you leave it empty the first time, it is made from your agency name. If you rename it, the old address stops working: visitors to it see a "page not found", and the old address does not redirect to the new one. Update the link on your website, and copy the button HTML again. A name that is taken or reserved is refused.
Turn off the switch and the address shows a "page not found" page. Leads you already have stay under Leads. Switch it back on whenever you like; the address does not change.
Every time platform support opened a read-only session on your agency, and why.
Platform support has not opened a session on your agency. If it does, the date, the person, the reason and how it ended are listed here.

Exited: support ended the session. Timed out: it reached 60 minutes. Replaced by a new session: support opened another one. Access revoked: the support person's platform access was removed during the session. Open means it has not ended yet.
Switch this on to get an email whenever platform support opens a session on your agency. The emails go to your agency admins. It is off until you turn it on.

A support session is when platform support opens your agency to help with a problem. A session lasts at most 60 minutes, is read-only so nothing can be changed, and starts with a reason you can read in this list. Everything done in a session is recorded in your agency's audit log.
How {assistant} words its recommendations, which starting-point rules apply and the settings behind them. Clients start from this runbook and can customise their own copy.

Each item has a badge that compares it with the standard runbook that came with the platform. Inherited means it matches; Customised means someone on your team changed it. Edit changes a play's title and template.

Clients whose business type has no built-in plays use this runbook directly. HVAC and dental clients keep the built-in plays until they get a runbook of their own. A client runbook is a copy of this one, with the plays tailored to the client. Changing this runbook does not rewrite a client's copy: the client shows Update available and chooses.
Only agency admins can change the agency runbook. Account managers can read it.

Plays are the recommendations a brief can suggest, each with a trigger and a template. Starting-point rules shape a client's first brief. Settings cover the alert and brief thresholds, focus services and competitor tiers. Switch an item off to leave it out.

When the standard runbook changes an item you inherited, it shows Update available. Review update shows what changed, and your own version if you customised it. Use the update takes the new text; Keep mine leaves yours as it is. A New item offers Add or Not now; one the standard runbook dropped offers Keep or Remove.
Post agency notices, such as a brief ready for review, to a Slack or Teams channel.
Add one below to post agency notices, such as a brief ready for review, to a Slack or Teams channel.

A webhook URL is a private web address that lets notices be posted to one channel. In Slack, create an incoming webhook for the channel and copy its URL (it starts with https://hooks.slack.com/). In Teams, create a Workflows or incoming webhook for the channel and copy its URL (the address ends in webhook.office.com, logic.azure.com or environment.api.powerplatform.com). Choose the matching Kind, paste the URL and choose Add webhook. Only https addresses on those hosts are accepted.

Tick the notices a channel should get, or tick none to send it all agency notices. The notices are: client alerts (agency), brief ready for review, brief failed, brief overdue, competitor suggestions ready, client updated their setup, setup waiting on you, quarterly report and rank scan skipped.
The Active switch stops posts to that channel without deleting the webhook. Switch it on again whenever you like.
The URL works like a password, so it is saved but never shown again: the table lists only its host. To change a URL, add a new webhook and switch the old one off.
Who can work in your agency and what they can do. Invite people by email and choose a role.
Invitations you send appear here until they are accepted or expire after 14 days.
The people you can manage appear here. Invite someone below with their email and a role.

An invitation is an email asking the person to sign in with that address; it works for 14 days. Each row shows when it was sent and when it expires. Resend emails it again and gives it another 14 days, up to 3 times a day. Revoke cancels it. Someone who already has access at that level cannot be invited again: remove them first to change their role.
Removing a person ends their access to this agency at once, and links already sent to them stop working. An agency needs at least one admin, so the last admin cannot be removed.

Agency admin: runs the agency, including billing, branding and the team. Account manager: works with clients, and can be limited to chosen clients. Client owner and Client viewer: people at one client; an owner can do more than a viewer, and both see only their own client. Admins manage everyone. Account managers manage the client owners and viewers of the clients they cover, so that is all they see here.

When you invite an account manager, tick the clients they cover, or tick none to cover all clients. An account manager who covers only some clients sees only those clients, and cannot add clients or prospects or see leads.
This month's credits used by each client against its monthly credit limit, with competitors and Ask questions. Months run on UTC.
Clients and prospects appear here with their credits, competitors and questions once you add them.
How many competitors the client tracks now, out of the most it may track. "Over limit" shows when it tracks more than its limit, for example after the limit was lowered.

The Ask questions the client's people have asked this UTC month, against the client's monthly quota. Only questions from client owners and viewers count; your own team's questions use none. At quota, the client's people cannot ask more until next month.

The status compares the client's credits with its limit. From 80% it reads Near limit. At 100% it reads Limit reached: nothing changes, and monitoring, briefs and Ask carry on as normal. Well past the limit, AI and monitoring work for that client pauses until the 1st of next month, and it reads Paused; past briefs and evidence stay available. The three tiles count the clients in each state.
Near limit, limit reached and paused

The AI and data work tied to the client so far this month, counted in credits against the client's monthly credit limit. The month is a UTC calendar month. Shared monitoring of a competitor (Google profile, reviews, ads, job posts) is split equally between the clients that track it. The intelligence engine's own shared work is not split across clients, so it is not in these figures. If you cover all clients, credits that are not tied to a client are listed under the table. Limits are set by the platform team; contact support to change one.
Ads your competitors run on Google and Meta, with when each one was first and last seen.
Try All platforms and All statuses, or another competitor. A competitor with no ads in the Google or Meta libraries has nothing to show.
How many ads each competitor had running on each weekly date, for the last 12 weeks. A week before a competitor's ads were first checked is left blank, not shown as zero.
An ad is active while the ad library still shows it (for Google ads, if it was shown in the last 14 days). Ended ads have stopped; each card shows when it was first and last seen.
The public ad libraries do not say who a US ad was aimed at, so each card reads "Targeting not disclosed (US)". Nothing on this page, and no brief, guesses at it.
A change important enough to send between weekly briefs, with the evidence behind it.
An alert is a change that was important enough to send straight away. Smaller changes wait for the weekly brief, and the smallest are only recorded. Every alert links to the evidence behind it.

The score is the change's score from 0 to 100; an alert is sent when it reaches the client's alert level (Settings › Alert rules). The status shows where the alert is in your review. "Template text" means the written text did not pass verification, so a fixed template was used instead.
Questions about your competitors and market, answered from the monitored evidence.
A saved conversation. It is private to you, and you can delete it from the list.

{assistant} answers from what has been monitored for {client}, such as changes, prices, ads and reviews. Facts link to their evidence. A sentence that starts with "Possible reason:" is an interpretation, not a stated fact. Sentences the evidence does not support are removed before you see the answer, and if there is no evidence for something, the answer says so.

{assistant} can propose saving a recommendation, changing a recommendation's status or rating a change. It shows a card with what it would do, and nothing happens until you confirm. Under an answer that cites evidence, "Save as recommendation" adds it to the Recommendations page.

Your questions and answers are private to you; other people at {client} or {agency} cannot open them. When a line under the box says conversations may be reviewed to improve answers, the people it names can read them. That line shows only while review is allowed for {client}. Delete a conversation with the bin icon beside it and confirm. While conversations may be reviewed, the people named in that line can still read it.
Four suggested questions, written from what competitors did in the last 7 days. Until the first set exists you see general ones. Pick one to ask it, or type your own.
{client}'s weekly briefs, alerts and quarterly reports, newest first.
What {client}'s competitors did, why it matters and what to do about it. Every point links to its evidence.

The percentage on each point shows how well the evidence supports it. Higher is better supported. "High confidence" marks the points we are most sure of, which also have an amber edge. Every point links to its evidence either way.
Each Evidence link opens the stored proof for the point above it: a snapshot, text or data captured from public information, with the date and a fingerprint that shows it has not been altered.

When no competitor made a significant move, the brief shows where {client} stands instead: rating, new reviews in the last 90 days, reply rate and share of top-3 map spots, each next to the median of the rivals we watch and the change since the starting point. The table lists every business.
The first brief. It shows where {client} stands against the competitors we watch on day one, and the first moves to make. Weekly briefs after it show what has changed since.

Numbers for {client} and each competitor over the period in the table caption: new reviews, average rating before and after, and ads running now. A dash in Active ads means not checked for that business.
Alerts are sent when a competitor makes an urgent change.
The first one arrives the Monday after setup is complete.
A report arrives in the first week after each quarter ends, and covers that quarter.

A weekly brief arrives on Monday morning: what changed, why it matters and what to do. An alert is a change important enough to send between briefs. A quarterly report gives the numbers for the quarter that just ended. A brief tagged Starting point is the first one, showing where {client} stands before weekly briefs begin.

The chip shows where each item stands in your review, such as Ready for review (briefs), Waiting for review (alerts), Approved or Sent; a report that could not be prepared shows Failed. Items waiting for review are in Approvals. Client users only see items that were delivered, and no chips.
Everything {client}'s competitors changed, scored for how much it matters. Every change links to its evidence.
Try a longer period, or All to include archived changes. A newly added competitor shows changes after its first checks.
Select a change on the left to see the evidence behind it and why it scored as it did.
Alert: important enough to send between briefs. Brief: goes in the weekly brief. Archived: recorded, but too small to report. Choose All or Archived to see everything that was found.

Alert at or above the alert level, Brief at or above the brief level, Archived below both. A change that still needs a check, or is too old to be urgent, goes to the brief instead of an alert. Change {client}'s levels under Settings › Alert rules.
Each change scores 0 to 100: 100 × type × size × relevance × novelty, each factor between 0 and 1. The line under the bars shows where alerts and the brief start.
The competitors monitored for {client}. Each one is rated by how closely it competes with {client}.
Everything monitored for this competitor: its prices, ads, reviews, local rankings and a timeline of changes.
Pages on the competitor's own website are found automatically and listed here once they are.

Each source monitored for this competitor, such as its Google profile or ads, and when it last ran. A note after the time, like "Not found" or "Retrying", describes that last run. "Paused" means the source is switched off.
How many of this competitor's moves are still open. A move is a pattern across several of its changes, such as a price war. Select the number to open the Moves page.

Pages on the competitor's own website that are checked for changes, such as prices, offers and service pages. "Site blocks monitoring" appears when the latest check of a page was refused by the site, so changes on it cannot be seen.
A pinned page is checked daily; other pages follow the default schedule for their type. Pages belong to the competitor, so pinning applies to every client that tracks it.
Accept a suggestion below or add one by name. A name is required; a website is optional.
Add one with the form below. A name is required; a website is optional.
No competitors are tracked for {client} yet. This session is read-only, so none can be added.

The day this competitor's tier and signals were last refreshed. It is a date, not a star rating: Google star ratings are on the Reviews page. "Not rated yet" means no tier has been worked out for it yet.

Businesses found by searching {client}'s service area, grouped by tier. Top rivals start ticked, up to the room left under the client's competitor limit. Dismiss hides one; "Show hidden" lists what the search left out and why. A search takes 20 to 40 minutes, and a client can have one manual search per week.

How closely a competitor competes with {client}. Top rival: it shows up in the same local searches and is active, with ads, new reviews or a claimed Google profile. Worth watching: strong on one of those. Minor: the rest. If a competitor's activity could not be checked, Worth watching is the highest tier it can get. The list starts with Top rivals.
The stored proof behind a point in a brief or alert: what was captured, when, and its fingerprint.

Pages on a competitor's own website are captured automatically by our monitoring service. Other sources, such as Google profiles and ad libraries, are recorded when their data is collected. Once stored, evidence is never edited.

A long code (a SHA-256 hash) worked out from the captured content. The same content always gives the same code, and changing even one character gives a completely different one. Working the code out again from the stored file and getting the same result shows it has not been altered since it was captured.
Evidence is kept under the retention policy, and for as long as a delivered brief cites it. Evidence on legal hold is never deleted.
Whether the capture worked. "ok" means the page or data was read normally.
Patterns across several changes, such as a competitor expanding, cutting prices or pushing ads. Each one is backed by the changes listed.
Moves are spotted from patterns in a competitor's changes, so a quiet stretch can have none.
A move is a pattern in one competitor's changes, such as a price war or an ad surge. It appears here when one is spotted. Choose Closed or All to see earlier ones.
Select a move on the left to see the changes behind it and their evidence.
A move is backed by changes: “3 changes” means three changes by this competitor fit the pattern. The list shows each one with its evidence. They are not the signal pills on the Competitors page.

Emerging: just spotted. Active: it has held for 7 days, or the evidence is strong. Fading: no new supporting change for 30 days. Closed: the pattern has not held for 30 days. Open covers every move that is not closed.
How {client} compares with its competitors this week.
The first brief arrives on a Monday morning. It covers what {client}'s competitors changed, why it matters and what to do.
Add competitors on the Competitors page to see how much pressure each one puts on {client}.
Your competitors appear here once {agency} has set them up.
A move is a pattern in a competitor's changes, such as a price war or an ad surge. Moves show here when one is spotted.
New recommendations come with each brief.
New recommendations come with each brief. You can also save one from an {assistant} answer.
A report arrives in the first week after each quarter ends.
Competitor ads running now on Google and Meta, where the ad libraries show them, compared with a week ago.
Competitor changes from the last 7 days that made the brief or an alert. The "high" pill counts how many of them were alerts.

How much each competitor has been doing lately, from 0 to 100: its changes from the last 30 days that made the brief or an alert, plus its open moves. The label reads High pressure (70 and above), Medium pressure (40 to 69), Low pressure (1 to 39) or Quiet (0). The line under each name is its main reason.
Competitor price changes from the last 7 days on services {client} offers, including small ones that did not make the brief. The pill counts the price cuts.
{client}'s Google rating next to the average rating of the tracked competitors.
The market picture shown to {client} before it became a client: its Google profile, ads and map visibility next to its competitors.

Figures only, straight from stored data, with no AI-written text. Rating, reviews and category come from the Google Business Profile, and ads running from the Google and Meta ad libraries. "Not checked" means there was no website or Meta page to look up.

Each cell reads "found/points · top 3 · avg". For one search term, found is the number of grid points where the business appeared, top 3 is how many of those it was in the first three, and avg is its average position at the points where it appeared. Unlike Local rankings, points where it did not appear are not counted as 21.
What each competitor charges on its website now, and how that changed. Pick a service to see its price history.
Add competitors on the Competitors page. Prices come from each competitor's own website.
Prices come from the competitors' own websites. A card fills in once a page that lists prices has been read; a competitor that does not publish prices stays empty.

Compares the competitor's lowest price for a service now with its lowest price 90 days ago. A red ▼ means the price fell and a green ▲ means it rose. The tag shows only when both prices are known and they differ, and it always looks back 90 days, whatever period you pick for the history. Promo marks a price listed as a promotion.
Marks a service {client} offers too, so you can compare like with like. It tags the service, not the price: every price on a card is the competitor's.
Where each business shows up in Google’s local results across {client}’s service area, from the weekly rank scan.
Scans run once a week, so Compare is available after the second one.
Add {client}'s Google Place ID on the Business profile page, or track a competitor, to see a grid.
The grid appears once {agency} has added {client}'s Google business or a competitor.
Add keywords and a service area on the Business profile page. The weekly scan then picks the client up, or you can start one with Scan now.
Rank tracking starts once {agency} has set up {client}'s keywords and service area.
Scans run once a week. The first one fills this page with a map of where {client} shows up in local results.

For one search term, the average position the business holds across all points of the grid; 1 is best. A point where the business is not in the first 20 results counts as 21. The line chart shows the average scan by scan.

Pick two scans to see the change at each point: blue means the business moved up, orange means it moved down, "=" means no change, and the number is how many places. Only scans with the same settings can be compared.

A square of search points spread across the service area; the page shows its size, such as 7×7. Each point is a Google Maps search made as if from that spot, and its cell shows where the business appeared in the first 20 results. Darker is better, 20+ means not in the first 20, and a hatched cell means no data for that point.

The weekly scan runs on Sundays at 06:00 UTC. Scan now starts an extra one. A client can be scanned by hand once every 7 days, and your agency can start 10 manual scans a day (counted per UTC day). A scan that would take the client past its monthly credit limit waits until next month. Rank settings change the keywords (up to 5), grid size and radius for the next scan.
A rank scan runs once a week. Every scan is kept, so you can follow the trend with the slider or compare two scans.

Of all the top-3 spots in a scan (the local pack, the map results Google shows first), across every grid point, the share each business holds. A business holding 12 of 60 spots has 20%. Businesses that are not tracked are grouped as "Other businesses".
Next steps from your weekly briefs and detected competitor moves.
Recommendations arrive with each approved weekly brief, and when a competitor move calls for a response.
Recommendations arrive with each approved weekly brief, and when a competitor move calls for a response. You can also save one from an {assistant} answer.
Rough estimates, shown as Low, Medium or High: how much work the step is (Effort) and how much it could help (Impact). They help you pick where to start. They are estimates, not measurements.

From weekly brief: the step is the recommended action of a brief item. From a detected move: it answers a pattern in a competitor's changes. From Ask: it was saved from an assistant answer. The evidence links on each card open the stored proof.
"For you" marks a step the business owner can take, such as asking customers for reviews. "Agency" marks a step {agency} can take. Agency users see "For you" as "Client".

To do, In progress and Done are the stages. Use Start, Done or Back to to-do on a card to move it. A dismissed recommendation goes to the list at the bottom with the reason given, and can be reopened. People with view-only access can read the board but not change it.
The numbers for one quarter: how {client} and its competitors compared, what changed and what was done about it.
This quarter had no data to report for {client}. The next report comes after the quarter ends.
Briefs sent and alerts delivered during the quarter, and the recommendations created in it, counted by where each one stood when the report was made: Done, In progress or Dismissed.

Reviews: new Google reviews in the last 90 days of the quarter. Average rating: the average stars over those 90 days; ▲ or ▼ shows it rose or fell compared with the 90 days before. Active ads: ads running when the report was made, shown only for competitors.
How many changes were scored for {client} during the quarter, grouped by type. Tiny cosmetic changes are left out.
Moves first detected during the quarter, with their status when the report was made. A move counts only while at least one change behind it is still valid.
What customers say about {client} and its competitors on Google.
Try another business, topic or star rating, or a longer period.

Rows are review topics; columns are businesses, {client} first. The number is the share of the reviews checked for that topic in the last 90 days that mention it. The color is how positive those mentions are: blue is positive, red is negative, gray is neutral. A dash means there are not enough reviews, and ▲▼ marks a change of 5 points or more since the previous 90 days.
Reviews posted on {client}'s Google profile in the last 90 days.
How many of {client}'s collected Google reviews gave 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 stars.

The average stars of the reviews posted in each month, for {client} and each competitor. A month without reviews has no point. With many competitors, some are combined into one "Other (average)" line.
Connect Claude, ChatGPT or another AI assistant to {client}'s competitor data. Answers come with the same evidence links you see here.
Paste the connector URL into Claude or ChatGPT and sign in. The app then shows up here.
Create one when a tool such as Claude Code needs access. Assistants you connect by signing in, like Claude or ChatGPT, do not need a token.

Agency roles do not create tokens on a client page. Agency-wide tokens live under Agency settings › AI connections, where a third level, Read, feedback and manage, is available. Here you see this client's tokens and connected apps; an admin sees everyone's.

Apps that were connected by signing in, rather than with a token. Each shows its permission level and which workspace it can reach. Disconnect removes its access straight away, and the app has to ask again next time.

Paste the connector URL into your AI assistant, then sign in and choose this workspace. Claude and ChatGPT add it from their Connectors settings. For Claude Code, create a token first and run the command shown.

Read only lets an assistant look things up. Read and feedback also lets it record feedback, such as changing a recommendation's status or rating a change. A token or connected app never gets more than your own role allows: owners can choose either level, viewers only Read only.

A token is a password for tools that cannot sign in, such as Claude Code or a script. It acts as you, with the permission level you choose. It is shown once when you create it, so copy it straight away. Revoke it at any time and anything using it stops working.
The score at which a competitor change becomes an instant alert or goes into the weekly brief.

A client gets at most 3 instant alerts a day, counted on the business's local day. Extra alerts wait for the evening digest, sent from 17:00 business time. How alerts are released is set under Delivery.

Every competitor change gets a score from 0 to 100 for how much it matters to {client}. At or above the alert level it is an instant alert; from the brief level up to the alert level it goes in the weekly brief; below the brief level it is archived but still listed under Changes. Both levels are whole numbers: brief 1 to 99, alert 2 to 100, with brief lower than alert. New levels apply to changes detected from now on.
The status of your plan, your next charge and your payment method.

Opens a secure payment page where you update your payment method and see your invoices, then brings you back here. The button appears once payment details exist; before that, use the payment link {agency} emailed you.
The date and amount of your next payment. If there is no next date, the page shows the monthly amount instead. When a plan is ending, it shows the day it ends rather than a charge.

Active: your plan is running. Payment needed: the last payment did not go through, so update your payment method. Awaiting payment setup: {agency} has emailed you a payment link. Cancelled: the plan is cancelled; if an end date is shown, that is the last day covered and there are no further charges. Paused: monitoring is paused, so contact {agency}. Not set up: billing has not been turned on for this workspace, so contact {agency}. Not available: your agency has not shared the billing details here; contact them.
How and when {client} receives alerts and briefs, in the business's own time zone, and who they go to.
Nobody receives this client's alerts or briefs yet. Add the owner's email below.

Direct sends each alert to the client at once. I review alerts first holds each alert for you to approve or dismiss before it is sent. Digest only never sends alerts one by one: they go out together in one digest from 17:00 business time. In every mode a client gets at most 3 instant alerts a day; any extra waits for that evening digest.

When on, a weekly brief that nobody has edited, dropped or reordered items in is approved and sent on Monday from 07:00 business time. A brief you touched waits for your approval, and you are told it is overdue.

The people who get this client's alerts and briefs. An Owner can also sign in and use whatever the client's features allow, including billing; a Viewer can only look. Each person can switch off kinds of message in their own preferences. Deactivating someone stops their messages, and links already sent to them stop working.

The clock for this client's deliveries: weekly briefs go out on Monday at 07:00, the evening digest from 17:00, quarterly reports from 08:00 in the first week of a quarter, and the 3-a-day alert limit counts each local day. It is the business's time zone, not your agency's.
The services, search keywords and service area used to find and compare {client}'s competitors.

A radius around the business, plus any ZIP codes and towns that are listed. “0 ZIP codes” means none are listed; the radius still applies. It decides which competitors are suggested and where local rankings are scanned.
Your agency keeps these details up to date because they decide which competitors are watched. If something is wrong, contact {agency}.

Which parts of the workspace the client can use: the dashboard, alert rules, managing competitors, the {assistant} and the AI connection page. A feature that is off is hidden from the client, not from your team. Allow review, for admins only, lets the platform team read this client's {assistant} conversations to improve answers.
Linked means {client}'s Google listing is connected, which lets us compare its reviews with its competitors'. Not linked means the listing still needs to be connected.
Services are what the business offers. Keywords are the searches customers use, up to 5, for example “ac repair”. Both are used to find competitors and to scan local rankings.
The plays, starting-point rules and settings used for this client’s briefs and recommendations.

Inherited means the item matches the agency runbook. Customised means someone on your team changed it for this client. Edit changes a play's title, template and the services it applies to; saving marks it Customised.

Until you create a runbook for this client, briefs use the agency runbook (HVAC and dental clients use the built-in plays) and this page is view-only. Creating one copies the agency items so you can tailor them. Only admins and account managers can edit.

Plays are the recommendations a brief can suggest, each with a trigger and a template. Starting-point rules shape the first brief. Settings cover the alert and brief thresholds, focus services and competitor tiers. Switch an item off to leave it out.

The agency runbook changed an item this client inherited. Review update shows what changed, and your own version if you customised it. Use the update takes the new text; for a play it is first tailored to this client, and you choose Approve or Use as is. Keep mine leaves the item as it is. A new item offers Add or Not now; one removed upstream offers Keep or Remove.
This month's credits for {client}'s monitoring, compared with the monthly limit. Months run on UTC.
Credits measure the monitoring and AI work done for {client} this month, against the monthly limit. The count starts again on the 1st of each month (UTC).

From 80% of the limit the page says Near limit. At 100% it says Limit reached: nothing changes, and monitoring, briefs and Ask carry on as normal. Well past the limit, monitoring and new briefs pause for the rest of the month and the page says Paused. Past briefs and evidence stay available, and your agency is told.
Near limit, limit reached and paused
Choose which nearby businesses {agency} should compare {client} with each week.
Get {client} ready for monitoring: confirm what they do and where, choose the competitors to watch, invite the owner and set up billing.

Instead of choosing, you can ask the owner to pick the competitors. You still invite them, because the invite is what emails them. The pick appears on their Overview. The starting-point brief waits for their choice, for at most 14 days.

The first brief, the starting point, shows where {client} stands next to its competitors. Its 48-hour wait starts when the competitors step is done (or setup is dismissed). It is made as soon as the business profile, reviews, first map scan and competitors are ready, or when those 48 hours are up. If setup never reaches the competitors step, the brief is held for at most 14 days after the client was added.

Up to 5 keywords, the searches customers use, and a search radius around the business. Competitor suggestions and local-ranking scans both use them. If the business has no Google listing, we place it from its address or from the City or ZIP you enter.

The first two screens, client details and finding the business, are on the Add a client page. Then: What they do and where, Pick who to watch, Invite the owner, Set up billing (clients only) and All set. Prospects skip billing. Save and exit keeps your progress and the setup reopens where you left off. Dismiss setup hides it; everything stays editable under Client settings and on the Competitors page.
Every agency with its live figures, health flag and billing state. Click a column heading to sort, or an agency name for its detail.
One agency: how it is doing, its team and clients, its billing and its recent support sessions.
Clients appear here once the agency adds them.
Archiving hides the agency and its clients from everyone outside the platform. Nothing is deleted, and an owner can unarchive it from the Archived filter. You can't archive while billing is active.

Shows the agency's billing state, plan and version, its trial and pilot end dates, how many seats Stripe has been told about ("sync pending" means an update is queued) and whether the agency is exempt from the pilot client limit. Owners and staff can grant or end a pilot, extend a trial and attach a discount code; only owners can lift the pilot client limit. Viewers read only.

Each client's spend this month, its effective monthly limit and its level. Leave the limit override blank to use the platform default. Competitors and Ask per month cap how many rivals a client can track and how many questions it can ask. Saving a higher limit lifts a spend pause when the client is back under the pause level. Owners and staff edit; viewers read only.
A hold makes the agency read-only, stops its scheduled work and pauses its billing. Its admins get an email when a hold starts and ends. Payments don't lift a hold; only staff can.
Everyone on this agency and its clients, plus invites that haven't been accepted. Staff can change agency roles, remove people and resend invites. Invites count toward the agency's daily limits.

View as agency opens a support session on this agency. It lasts 60 minutes, is read-only, and needs a reason of 5 to 300 characters that the agency can read. Only platform owners and staff can start one. Every session is recorded in the agency's audit log and listed under Support sessions below.
Agencies appear here when they sign up, either through open sign-up or an invite link from Billing & plans.

Pilot: on a free pilot. Free trial: on its trial. Active: paying. Payment overdue: a payment failed, or a trial or subscription ended unpaid. Read-only: the agency has been read-only since it was 7 days overdue. Suspended: 30 days after Read-only begins. Cancelled: the subscription ended.

Active clients are active and not paused. Prospects are clients not yet active. Seats are people with an agency role plus people with a client role. WAU is people active in the last 7 days. Last activity is the latest activity by anyone in the agency, client users included; a dash means none yet. Spend this month is AI and data cost recorded against the agency since the 1st (UTC). Click a heading to sort: Agency and Health start A to Z (at risk first), the others start with the highest or newest.

The first rule that matches wins. At risk: the agency is at least 28 days old and nobody on its agency team has been active in the app for 14 days (or ever), or it has fewer active clients than 28 days ago. Idle: at least 14 days old, has an active client and has sent no brief in the last 14 days. Growing: at least 28 days old with more active clients than 28 days ago. Steady: anything else, including every agency under 14 days old. The 28-day comparison is skipped when no figures were stored for that day.
Active includes agencies on hold. Archived agencies can be restored by an owner, and purged after 30 days.
Conversations from clients that allow review. Opening one is recorded in the audit log.
Conversations appear here once a client that allows review has asked the assistant a question.
A read-only copy of one conversation, as text only. Opening it was recorded in the audit log.
Each message shows its role (user, assistant or action) and a status: ok, quota (the question allowance was used up), refused, error or cancelled.

Citations lists what a reply relied on; a kb: citation links to its knowledge article. Trace, where a message has one, is the assistant's own log of how it answered, and an action block is the raw detail of an action message. Both are shown as plain text.

Only conversations of clients whose profile allows platform review. A client that has not allowed it never appears here, and its threads cannot be opened by id either. The list is newest first, 25 at a time.
Every time you open a conversation, a row is written to the agency's audit log with your name and the time. Listing them is not recorded; opening is.

N removed: sentences the answer check removed from replies. Something went wrong: a reply failed. Couldn't answer: the assistant declined a question. Limit reached: the client ran out of its question allowance. Deleted by user: the person removed it from their list; it stays here for review.
Revenue and plans in five tabs: Overview (MRR, paid seats, agencies by billing state), Plans, Discount codes, Sign-up & invites and Stripe Connect.

A code takes a percentage or a dollar amount off the base price, the seats or both, for the first invoice, for 1 to 36 months, or forever. It can have an expiry date and a maximum number of uses. Only owners can create or revoke a code.

Agencies bill their own clients through their own Stripe account. The default fee is the percentage the platform takes from those payments; an agency can have its own override, and a blank override goes back to the default. 0 sends no fee. A change applies to Checkout links created afterwards; existing subscriptions keep the fee they started with. Only owners can change fees.

An invite link lets an agency sign up on a pilot or a trial. Max uses is 1 to 1,000. The link expires in 1 to 90 days (14 if you leave it blank). A pilot link needs a pilot end date after the day the link expires. The full link is shown once, right after you create it, and cannot be retrieved later. Lock to email limits it to one address, and you can email it from here. Owners and staff only.
Monthly recurring revenue and the number of paid seats, summed over all agencies from the latest daily stats, so they can be up to a day behind.

Each row is one version of the plan. Publishing a new version makes it current for new subscriptions; existing subscriptions keep their prices. Trial days is the length of a new trial. Only owners can publish a version.

To limit a code to certain agencies, paste their agency ids (UUIDs) into the box, separated by commas or spaces, up to 100. An agency's id is the long code at the end of its page address, /platform/agencies/<id>. Every id must belong to an existing agency or the code is refused. A restricted code has no promotion code, so agencies cannot type it at checkout: attach it from the agency's page instead. It cannot go on an invite link.

When open sign-up is paused, new agencies cannot sign themselves up; invite links keep working. Only owners can change it. The funnel counts agencies that reached each step in the last 30 or 90 days: signed up, finished their profile, added a first client, added a card, split by open sign-up and invite link.
What it costs to run the platform: vendor balances, monthly spend and manual costs. API balances refresh daily at 06:00 UTC.
AI calls tied to a business type in the last 30 days appear here with their cost.
Add costs the vendors cannot report, such as a hosting plan or a subscription, so the monthly totals are complete.

AI calls and their cost over the last 30 days, grouped by the business type they were for. A business type that was merged is counted under the one it was merged into, and a draft not yet created shows as a draft.
About AI cost by business type

Platform-wide defaults for AI spend: the credits rate shown to agencies and clients, the default monthly limit per client, the percentage of that limit at which a client is paused, and the spike guard's warn and pause levels, daily floors and snooze time. Only the fields you change are saved. A client's own limit is set on its agency page.

When a service turns Low, platform owners are emailed once; the email is sent again only after the service has been OK and turned Low again. While any service is Low, owners also see a strip at the top of every platform page. The Warnings card counts the Low services.

Costs the vendors cannot report, such as hosting or a subscription. A monthly item counts every month, a yearly item counts one twelfth each month, and a one-off item counts in the month it starts. Archiving an item keeps it in past months' totals and stops it counting later.

The last six months, API usage and manual costs stacked. It is approximate: for balance services the spend is the sum of the drops between daily readings (top-ups are ignored), and a month with fewer than two readings counts as zero. Usage services use their last reading of the month.
API spend so far this month divided by the days elapsed, times the days in the month, plus the manual costs for the month. It is a straight-line guess and moves a lot early in the month.

OK: enough left. Low: the balance is under its low-balance threshold, or the days left are at or under the warning window (7 days unless you changed it). Error: the last reading failed. Unavailable on this plan: the vendor does not report this figure. Not configured: no reading yet. Off: tracking is switched off. Days left comes from how fast the balance fell over the last 14 days; with fewer than two readings it is blank.
Is the worker alive, are jobs flowing, and are the data sources fresh. The spend guard shows whether AI work is running normally. Spend totals live under Costs.

One row per job queue. Slow: the oldest waiting job is over 30 minutes old, or a job failed in the last 24 hours. Down: the oldest waiting job is over 2 hours old. If the queue database cannot be read, the table says so and the worker shows Down.
When data last arrived: the newest successful vendor call and the newest successful web capture. Slow: over 26 hours ago. Down: over 72 hours ago, or never.

Watches AI spend against its normal level for each provider and for all providers together. Warning: spend is above normal by the warn percentage. Paused: it is above normal by the pause percentage, so all AI calls are held and queued work waits. A "floor" marker means the reading is too small in dollars to trigger anything. Staff and owners can Reset with a short note; the guard then stays quiet for the snooze period. Clients paused for reaching their own limit are listed below.
Vendors called in the last 48 hours. Slow: 20% or more of the calls in the last 24 hours failed. Down: 50% or more failed, or none succeeded in 48 hours.
The background worker records a heartbeat every 5 minutes. Working: the last one is under 11 minutes old. Slow: 11 to 30 minutes. Down: over 30 minutes, or no heartbeat yet.
Articles the Ask assistant can search and cite, at platform, agency and client level.
Read or edit one article. Publish saves a change to a published article and queues it for the assistant's search index; Save draft takes it out of search.

With auto-sync on, the article is re-read from its web address every Sunday at 05:00 UTC and updated when the page changed; the text before the last change is kept under Previous version. A sync error is shown in red. Turning auto-sync off keeps the current text.
Delete removes the article and its search index and cannot be undone. To take an article out of search but keep it, unpublish it instead.
This article is seeded from the repository, so it is shown read-only. To change it, edit its Markdown in the repo and run kb:seed again.
Write one with New article, or import one from a web address. Published articles can be found and cited by the assistant.
Write an article the Ask assistant can search and cite. Pick who it belongs to, write it in Markdown, then keep it as a draft or publish it.

Choose the level (and the agency or client it belongs to), the kind, a title and the Markdown body. The Preview tab shows how it reads. Save draft keeps it out of search; Publish makes it findable by the assistant.

For an agency-level article, "Visible to client users" decides whether that agency's clients can read it as well as its staff. It is on by default. Platform and client-level articles do not show the option.

Level says who the article belongs to: Help (platform) for everyone, Agency for one agency, Client for one client. Kind is its type: help article, playbook, Q&A, blog post or fact. Use the filters to narrow the list.
Articles badged "Managed in repo" are the page guides and glossary terms seeded from the repository by kb:seed. They are read-only here: change the Markdown in the repo and seed again.
Only Published articles can be found and cited by the assistant. A Draft stays out of search until it is published.

An article imported from a web address (when URL import is switched on) can sync itself: it is re-read every Sunday at 05:00 UTC and updated if the page changed. The badge shows the last sync, "changed" when the text changed, or the reason a sync failed.
Verified requests from the platform page that no agency holds yet. Assign one to an agency; it is notified by email.
The 20 most recent assignments appear here.
Verified requests from the platform page appear here until an agency is given them.
A lead marked "Declined by an agency" was given to an agency that sent it back. It is in the pool again and can go to a different agency.

Choose an agency and press Assign. Each agency in the list shows its active business types and active client count, so you can match the lead. The agency is emailed and the lead leaves the pool. Only owners and staff can do this, and an agency that already holds the same visitor and business is refused.
Giving a lead to an agency

Requests from the platform's own page whose email address is verified and that no agency holds. The list is newest first, 25 at a time; use Previous and Next for more. A lead stays here until an agency is given it.
How the platform is doing: agencies, active clients, seats, weekly active users and this month's spend, with charts for the last 12 weeks or 12 months and the latest activity.
Events appear here as agencies sign up, add and activate clients, send a first brief, become at risk or have a support session opened.

Newest first, 20 at a time (Show more loads the next 20). It lists an agency signing up, adding or activating a client, sending its first brief, becoming at risk, and a support session being opened on it.

Agencies: every agency on the platform. Active clients: clients with status active that are not paused. Seats: the people with an agency role plus the people with a client role. Weekly active users: people who used the app in the last 7 days, today included. Spend this month: AI and data cost recorded against an agency since the 1st of the month (UTC); cost not tied to one agency is not in it.

Each big number is today's live figure. The small pill beside it is the change since 28 days ago, taken from the daily figures stored then. No pill means no change, or nothing was recorded 28 days ago. For Spend this month the pill compares the month so far with the month-to-date total as it stood 28 days ago.

The toggle changes the charts, not the figures above them. 12 weeks shows one point per week (weeks start on Monday); 12 months shows one point per month. A gap in a line means nothing was recorded for that period.
Decisions the models weren’t sure about. Your answer fixes the event and becomes a gold label.
When the models cannot settle a decision with enough confidence, it appears here for you to answer.

Each card shows the text before and after a competitor change, with one or more questions. "Model said" is the model's answer and its confidence; yours replaces it. Your answers fix the event and are stored as gold labels for measuring the models. The queue is oldest first, 25 at a time; use Previous and Next for more.

Competitor changes are classified by a cascade. Jev answers first; any answer under 0.85 confidence goes to a language model; if that answer is also under 0.85, the question lands here for a person. The brief verifier uses the same 0.85 threshold.
The standard plays, starting-point rules and settings every agency starts from. Agencies see your changes as updates they can take or keep their own version.
Platform owners and staff can edit the standard runbook. Viewers can read it. Nobody can edit in a read-only support session.

This is the runbook every agency starts from: plays (the recommendations a brief can suggest), starting-point rules and settings. Each agency gets its own copy, and each client can in turn get a copy of the agency's.

Changing an item here does not rewrite an agency's copy. The agency's item shows Update available, and its admins choose to use the update or keep their own version. An item you add shows as New, and one you remove shows as Removed upstream.
New review topics found in reviews that didn’t fit any existing topic. An approved topic is asked for every new review, and reviews from the last 180 days are checked for it too.
When enough reviews fit none of a business type's topics, a proposed new topic appears here for you to approve or reject.

Approve a topic and it is asked for every new review in that business type, and reviews from the last 180 days are checked for it in the background. Reject it and it is not proposed again. A decision cannot be undone from this page, and a proposal someone else already decided shows an error.
The table lists proposals approved or rejected in the last 30 days, with the business type, the decision and the date.

Each night, for every business type, reviews that matched no topic are collected. With at least 20 of them from the last 90 days since the last proposal, a model looks for one recurring topic that at least a fifth of them share, and proposes it. A business type has one open proposal at a time. "N reviews with no topic" is how many it looked at.
New business types and services agencies added. Approve what is right, fix what is not, or merge duplicates into an existing entry.
When an agency adds a service to a business type, it appears here for you to approve, rename or merge.
When an agency creates a new business type, it appears here for you to approve, fix or merge.

Approve marks a business type reviewed, together with the services it came with, or a single service reviewed. Rename changes the name and keeps the id. Edit (business types only) changes the keywords, Google categories, review topics and services before you approve. A name cannot include a client's business name, phone number, email or web address.

Merge into moves everything of the duplicate to the entry you pick: its clients, events, prices and agency settings. The old id keeps resolving to the target. For a business type you also say where each of its services goes; matching names are pre-filled and "Move" keeps a service as a new one. A service merges into another service of the same business type.

Business types and services that agencies created while setting up a client and that nobody has reviewed yet, with who added them, how many clients use them and the evidence behind them. The number on the menu item counts both lists.
Platform owners and staff can approve, rename, edit and merge. Viewers can read the queue and the evidence but see no buttons.
People who joined the pilot waitlist from the public website. Invite agencies, pass businesses to an agency and build sample briefs.
Agencies that join the waitlist from the public website appear here.
Local businesses that join the waitlist from the public website appear here.
Agencies that ask for a sample brief when they join appear here.
Nothing on the waitlist matches that search.
Only entries whose email address is confirmed can be invited, assigned or given a sample. Unconfirmed entries are shown so you can see demand.
Approving a sample creates the business in the Samples agency and opens its setup. Run setup as usual, approve the starting point in Approvals, then press Send sample here.
Set to cancel at period end

# Asking {{assistant}} about a client's competitors

{{assistant}} answers questions about a client's competitors and market, using the evidence {{product}} has collected from public information.

## Where to ask

- On a client's Overview page, the **Ask {{assistant}}** card lists suggested questions. Select one to open it in the assistant, or choose **Open** to start with your own question.
- You can also go straight to the client's Ask page. Past conversations are listed beside the chat so you can return to them or delete them.

Ask is available when it is switched on for your plan and role.

## Evidence in answers

Answers cite the evidence they rely on. Look for the numbered evidence chips in the answer, and select one to see the original snapshot or text.

## Saving an answer as a recommendation

Under an answer you can choose **Save as recommendation**. A dialog opens with a suggested title and rationale that you can edit before saving. The evidence the answer cited is attached to the recommendation.

## Confirm before anything changes

The assistant does not change anything on its own. If it proposes a change, such as saving a recommendation, a card shows what it will do, with **Confirm** and **Cancel** buttons. Nothing is saved until you confirm. After you decide, the conversation shows a short note such as "Saved." or "Cancelled."

## Tips

- Name the competitor or the topic you care about.
- Ask follow-up questions in the same conversation to build on an answer.
- Treat the cited evidence as the source of truth, and open it when a detail matters.

# Connect an AI app to {{product}}

You can connect an AI app such as Claude, ChatGPT or Claude Code to {{product}}. The app can then answer questions about your clients' competitors using the same monitored evidence you see in the dashboard.

Connections are for agency staff. Open **Agency settings › AI connections** (`/agency/settings/ai`). Each client also has its own **AI connection** tab under **Client settings**.

## The connector URL

The top card shows your connector URL. It is your app address followed by `/mcp`. Use the Copy button to copy it.

- **Claude** (claude.ai or the desktop app): go to Settings, then Connectors, then Add custom connector. Paste the URL, sign in and choose this workspace.
- **ChatGPT**: go to Settings, then Connectors, and create a connector in developer mode. Paste the URL and sign in.
- **Claude Code**: create an access token first (see below), then add the URL with the command shown on the page, using your token in the Authorization header.

Once connected, the app can reach every client you have access to. When it matters, it asks which client you mean.

## Access tokens

Some tools need a personal access token instead of a sign-in. Create one in the Access tokens card and choose how much it may do:

- **Read only**
- **Read and feedback**
- **Read, feedback and manage** (available only if your role allows it)

A new token is shown once. Copy it straight away, because you cannot see it again. Admins see every member's tokens and connected apps in the agency.

## Taking access away

- To stop a token working, choose **Revoke** next to it. Anything using it stops straight away.
- Apps connected by sign-in appear in the Connected apps card, where you can revoke them in the same way.

## What this page tells you

Alerts that are waiting for you, for clients whose alert mode is **I review alerts first**. Each card shows the client, the competitor, the alert's **Score**, the headline and text, and how many evidence items back it.

## What this page tells you

The weekly briefs for all your clients. {{assistant}} drafts each client's brief on Thursday night, in the client's time zone. You review and approve it for Monday 07:00. The list shows this week's brief for each client, plus any older brief that is still waiting.

- **Status** is one of **Ready for review** (drafted and waiting for you), **Approved** (it goes out Monday 07:00), **Sent**, **Drafting** (still being written) or **Failed — retrying**.
- **Items** shows how many items are still in the brief and how many were removed, by the fact-check or by you.

1. **Open the briefs that say Ready for review.** Click the client's name.
2. **Review each item** against its evidence, edit or remove what you do not want, then approve.
3. **Turn on auto-send** for a client whose briefs you trust, from the bottom of its review page.

A client's brief is only sent by approval or auto-send. You can also send one at once from its review page.

## Common questions

### What does the client get if I do nothing?

A brief that you have not approved is not sent, unless the client is set to auto-send and you have not touched the draft.

### Why is there no brief for a client?

Briefs are drafted on Thursday night in the client's time zone. A client that has just been added, or is paused, may not have one yet.

### Where do alerts that need review go?

Alerts held for your check are under Alert review, not here.

## What this page tells you

One client's brief, ready for your check before the client sees it. A banner at the top says every remaining sentence was checked against saved evidence, and how many sentences or items the fact-check removed because it could not prove them.

Each item shows what changed, why it matters and a suggested action, with chips that open the evidence. At the right of an item:

- **Confidence** is a percentage for how sure the draft is about the item. At 85% and above it reads **High confidence** and the item gets an amber edge; below that it reads **Confidence**. It is a prompt to look closer, not a verdict.
- **Upsell** appears when the item points to a service you could sell. Only you see it: it is never part of the brief the client reads.
- **Dropped** marks an item that was removed. It is left out of the brief the client sees.

A starting-point brief, the first one for a new client, also shows a **Where you stand** scorecard.

## How to use it

1. **Read each item** and open its evidence if something looks off.
2. **Edit** the headline, what changed, why it matters or the suggested action. **Remove** an item you do not want, with an optional reason. Use the arrows to reorder.
3. **Rate** items **Useful** or **Not useful**. You can do this at any time, even after the brief is sent.
4. **Approve** the brief. It is scheduled for Monday 07:00 in the client's time zone, and its items become the client's recommendations. A starting-point brief is sent as soon as you approve it.
5. **Send now** instead if it should go out at once. It approves the brief if needed and sends it to the client's recipients.
6. **Auto-send** is a switch at the bottom: with it on, untouched briefs go out on Monday 07:00 without your approval.

**Client view** opens the brief the way the client will read it.

## Common questions

### Why can I not edit this brief?

You can edit while it says **Ready for review**. Once it is approved or sent, items can no longer be edited, removed or reordered.

### Does the client see what I removed?

No. Removed items are left out of the brief the client sees.

### What is a quiet week?

A week with no significant competitor moves. The page says so and the brief has few or no items.

Billing is for agency admins. Account managers and client roles get a "not found" page.

Work tied to a client is included, plus an equal share of each competitor's shared monitoring for every client that tracks it. The intelligence engine's own shared work is not split across clients.

It tracks more competitors than its current limit, for example after the limit was lowered. Remove competitors from the client's Competitors page.

### The Health flag

The first rule that matches wins:

- **At risk**: the agency is at least 28 days old and nobody on its agency team has been active in the app for 14 days (or ever), or it has fewer active clients than 28 days ago.
- **Idle**: at least 14 days old, has an active client and has sent no brief in the last 14 days.
- **Growing**: at least 28 days old with more active clients than 28 days ago.
- **Steady**: anything else, including every agency under 14 days old.

The 28-day comparison is skipped when no figures were stored for that day. "Active in the app" for the At risk rule means the agency team (admins and account managers); Last activity counts everyone.

### Billing states

Past due means a payment failed, or a trial or subscription ended unpaid. An agency that stays 7 days past due becomes Paused (read-only); 30 days after that it becomes Suspended.

### Status filters

Above the table, **Active**, **On hold**, **Archived** and **All** filter the list; On hold and Archived show how many agencies each holds. Active includes agencies on hold, which show an On hold chip.
