## What this page tells you

Revenue, plans and sign-up controls for the whole platform. Everyone with platform access can read it; owners change things, staff can create invite links, viewers read only.

The page has five tabs: **Overview**, **Plans**, **Discount codes**, **Sign-up & invites** and **Stripe Connect**. Pausing sign-ups, publishing a plan version, revoking a code or link and changing a Connect fee each ask you to confirm first.

- **MRR** and **Paid seats** are summed over all agencies from the latest daily stats, so they can be up to a day behind.
- **Agencies by state** counts agencies in each billing state: Pilot, Trial, Active, Past due, Paused, Suspended and Cancelled. Past due becomes Paused after 7 days, and Paused becomes Suspended 30 days later.
- **Sign-up & invites** has the **Agency sign-up** panel, which shows whether open sign-up is open or paused (invite links work either way) and a funnel for the last 30 or 90 days: sign-ups, profiles completed, first clients added and cards added, split by open sign-up and invite link.
- **Plans** lists every plan version. A new version becomes current for new subscriptions; existing subscriptions keep their prices. Trial days is the length of a new trial. Each version also shows what it includes (Ask, MCP access), set with checkboxes when you publish; the form starts from the current version's choices.
- **Agencies not on the current version** sits under the plans table. It lists each agency still on an older version (or with none set), its state and its monthly price now and after a move. Owners tick agencies and choose **Move selected to `v{N}`** (the current version); agencies on hold cannot be ticked.
- **Discount codes** take a percentage or a dollar amount off the base price, the seats or both, for the first invoice, for 1 to 36 months, or forever, with an optional expiry date and maximum number of uses.
- **Stripe Connect** shows how many agencies have connected Stripe, their paying clients and client MRR, and the platform fee. An agency can have its own fee; leave it blank to use the default; 0 sends no fee. A change applies to Checkout links created afterwards.
- **Agency invite links**, below it on the same tab (owners and staff), lists links by their first characters only.

## How to use it

1. **Pause or resume open sign-up** (owners) when you need to stop new agencies signing up themselves.
2. **Publish a plan version** (owners) with a name, base price, included seats, extra seat price and trial days.
3. **Move agencies to the current version** (owners): tick the agencies, then Move selected. The dialog shows each agency's price now and after, and warns when the new version includes fewer seats than the agency has active clients (a paid agency pays for the extra seats; a pilot or full-trial agency can't activate new clients until it is under the limit). Feature changes apply at once. A live subscription gets the new prices from its next billing date, with no proration. Agency admins are emailed when their price or features change. The result says how many moved and names any that did not, with the reason.
4. **Create a discount code** (owners). To limit it to certain agencies, paste their **agency ids** in the box, separated by commas or spaces, up to 100. An agency's id is the long code at the end of its page address, `/platform/agencies/<id>`. Every id must belong to an existing agency or the code is refused.
5. **Create an invite link** (owners and staff): choose Pilot or Trial, a pilot end date for pilots, an optional discount code, an optional email to lock it to (you can email it from here), max uses (1 to 1,000), expiry (1 to 90 days, 14 if blank) and a note. Copy the link straight away: it is shown once and cannot be retrieved later.
6. **Set Connect fees** (owners) for everyone or for one agency.

## Common questions

### Why can't a restricted code go on an invite link?

The agency created from a link does not exist yet, so a code limited to named agencies could never apply. A restricted code also has no promotion code, so agencies cannot type it at checkout; attach it from the agency's page (or the agency's Redeem form).

### Why must a pilot end after the link expires?

The pilot has to outlast the link. The form warns you before you submit: it asks for a later pilot end date or a shorter expiry.

### What does revoking do?

A revoked link or code can no longer be used.

### Why is MRR zero?

MRR comes from the newest daily stats row. On a fresh environment it stays zero until the nightly job has run.

## What this page tells you

What it costs to run {{product}}: vendor balances, monthly spend and manual costs. Only platform owners can open it. Vendor balances refresh daily at 06:00 UTC; **Refresh now** queues a refresh, and the button shows Refreshing while one is queued.

- **Spent this month** is API spend so far plus manual costs for the month. **Projected this month** is API spend so far divided by the days elapsed, times the days in the month, plus manual costs; it moves a lot early in the month. **Warnings** counts the services that are Low.
- **Services** lists each vendor with a status: **OK**; **Low** (the balance is under its low-balance threshold, or the days left are at or under the warning window, 7 days unless changed); **Error** (the last reading failed); **Unavailable on this plan** (the vendor does not report this figure); **Not configured** (no reading yet); **Off** (tracking is switched off). Days left comes from how fast the balance fell over the last 14 days, and is blank with fewer than two readings.
- **Monthly spend** shows the last six months, API usage and manual costs stacked. It is approximate: for balance services the spend is the sum of drops between daily readings (top-ups are ignored), and a month with fewer than two readings counts as zero. Usage services use their last reading of the month.
- **AI by business type (last 30 days)** shows AI calls and cost per business type. A merged business type is counted under the one it was merged into.
- **Limits & spike guard** (owners only) holds the settings that decide when AI work is limited: how many credits equal $1 (tenants see credits, you see dollars), the default monthly limit per client, the percentage of a client's limit at which its AI and monitoring work pauses, the warn and pause percentages for an AI spend spike, the two daily spend floors that stop tiny numbers from triggering the guard, and how long the guard stays quiet after a reset. Only the fields you change are saved.
- **Manual costs** are costs the vendors cannot report. A monthly item counts every month, a yearly item one twelfth a month, a one-off item in the month it starts. Archiving keeps past months' totals.

## How to use it

1. **Check Warnings.** When a service turns Low, owners are emailed once (again only after it recovers and turns Low again), and a strip shows at the top of every platform page.
2. **Edit a service** to set its billing link, low-balance threshold and warning window. Some services need a dollars-per-unit rate before they can warn. Usage services without a plan cap never warn.
3. **Add manual costs** with the dialog under Manual costs; Archive ends a recurring cost.
4. **Watch Projected this month** against what you expect to pay.
5. **Change a guard setting** in Limits & spike guard and save. A client's own limit is set on its agency page under Client limits, not here.

## Common questions

### Why does a service say Not configured?

The worker has not written a reading yet. Only the worker holds the vendor credentials.

### Why is days left blank?

There are fewer than two balance readings in the last 14 days, or the balance did not fall.

### Why does saving a guard setting say Nothing to change?

No field differs from what is stored. A field left with text that is not a number is refused with Enter numbers only.

### Why don't these numbers match the Overview page?

Overview's spend is only cost recorded against an agency. This page is what the vendors charge the platform.

## What this page tells you

Whether the platform is running: the background worker, its job queues, the data vendors and how fresh the collected data is. Each row has a status: **Working**, **Slow** or **Down**. Vendor balances and spend totals live on the Costs page; the **Spend guard** card below shows whether AI work is running normally.

- **Worker:** when the background worker last recorded a heartbeat. Slow after 11 minutes, Down after 30 minutes or with no heartbeat.
- **Queues:** jobs waiting, running and failed in the last 24 hours, per queue. Slow when the oldest waiting job is over 30 minutes old or a job failed; Down over 2 hours.
- **Vendors:** calls and errors in the last 24 hours for each vendor called in the last 48 hours. Slow at 20% errors; Down at 50%, or with no successful call in 48 hours.
- **Sources:** the newest successful vendor call and web capture. Slow after 26 hours; Down after 72 hours or never.
- **Spend guard:** compares the last 24 hours of AI spend with its normal level, for all providers together and for OpenRouter and Anthropic separately. **OK** is normal; **Warning** means spend is above normal by the warn percentage; **Paused** means it is above normal by the pause percentage, so every AI call is held and queued work waits. A scope marked *floor* is too small in dollars to trigger anything. The card also lists clients paused for reaching their own monthly limit, and the last 50 guard events. The guard checks hourly.

## How to use it

1. **Start with the worker.** If it is Down, nothing else moves: queues fill up and sources go stale.
2. **Then the queues.** A queue on Slow with failures points at one job type; the error tracker (Open Sentry, when configured) has the details.
3. **Then vendors and sources.** A vendor on Down usually means an outage or an expired key; check its balance on Costs.
4. **If the spend guard shows Paused,** find out why spend jumped (the vendor call counts on Costs and the error tracker help), then use **Reset** (owners and staff). Reset asks for a short note of up to 200 characters, resumes queued AI work, and keeps the guard quiet for the snooze period, so a reading at pause level only warns during that time. Reset is not offered when the guard is OK.

## Common questions

### Why does a queue show Slow when nothing is waiting?

A job in that queue failed in the last 24 hours. The status clears once a day passes without failures.

### Why is there no Open Sentry link?

The link appears only when error tracking is configured for this deployment.

### Why is a client paused when the platform guard is OK?

The client went well past its own monthly limit. That pause is separate from the platform guard: it lifts on the 1st of next month, or when you raise the client's limit on the agency page (Client limits).

### Who can open it?

Platform owners, staff and viewers. Only owners and staff can Reset.

## What this page tells you

One article, open for reading or editing. The page title is the article's title.

- **A manual or URL article** shows the editor: title, level, kind, Markdown body with Preview, and Save draft, Publish and Unpublish buttons.
- **A Managed in repo article** (page guides and glossary terms seeded from the repository) shows a "Managed in repo" notice and the rendered article, read-only.
- **A URL article** also shows its source address, an **Auto-sync** switch, any sync error in red and, once it has changed, the **Previous version**.

## How to use it

1. **Edit and publish.** **Publish** saves your change to a published article, re-indexes it and queues it for the search index, so the assistant finds the new text shortly after. **Save draft** takes it out of search until you publish again.
2. **Turn auto-sync on or off** for a URL article. With it on, the page is re-read every Sunday at 05:00 UTC and the text updated if it changed. Turning it off keeps the current text.
3. **Unpublish** to take the article out of search but keep it.
4. **Delete** removes the article and its search index and cannot be undone; you are asked to confirm.

## Common questions

### Why is there no editor?

The article is Managed in repo. Change its Markdown in the repository and seed again.

### What is a sync error?

The page could not be fetched, or its site does not allow it. The message in red says which.

## What this page tells you

A form for writing an article the Ask assistant can search and cite.

- **Level** says who the article belongs to: Help (platform), Agency or Client. Agency and Client levels also ask which agency (and client).
- **Kind** is the type: help article, playbook, Q&A, blog post or fact.

## How to use it

1. **Choose the level and kind**, then write the title and body.
2. **Check the Preview** tab to see how the Markdown reads.
3. **Save draft** keeps it out of the assistant's search. **Publish** makes it findable.
4. After the first save the page may show warnings about the text; read them before publishing.

## Common questions

### Can I use the product name?

For a platform-level article, write the product name as `{{product}}` and the assistant's name as `{{assistant}}`, so white-label agencies see their own. The editor warns when it finds the literal names.

### Where do page guides come from?

They live in the repository (`docs/help/pages`) and are seeded, not written here.

## What this page tells you

Articles the Ask assistant can search and cite, at three levels: **Help (platform)** for everyone, **Agency** for one agency, **Client** for one client. Each article has a kind: help article, playbook, Q&A, blog post or fact.

Badges on each row:

- **Draft** or **Published**. Only Published articles can be found and cited by the assistant.
- **Manual**, **URL** or **Managed in repo**. Managed in repo articles are the page guides and glossary terms seeded from the repository by `kb:seed`. They are read-only here.

## How to use it

1. **Filter** by level, agency, client, kind or status, or search titles.
2. **Click New article** to write one, or open a row to edit it.
3. **To change a Managed in repo article**, edit its Markdown in the repo and seed again.
4. **URL import** (when it is switched on) fetches a web page as a draft. With auto-sync on, the article is re-read every Sunday at 05:00 UTC and updated if the page changed.
5. **Page through** with Older articles; 25 show at a time.

## Common questions

### Why can't I edit an article?

It is Managed in repo. Its source is a Markdown file in the repository.

### Why can't the assistant find my article?

It is probably a Draft. Publish it. The search index is built in the background by an hourly sweep, so a newly published article can take up to an hour to be found.

### Can an agency's clients read an agency-level article?

That is set per article with **Visible to client users** (on by default).

## What this page tells you

Verified requests from the platform's own request page that no agency holds yet. Only requests whose email address is verified appear. The list is newest first, 25 at a time, with Previous and Next links.

Each row shows the business, its address and category, the visitor's message and contact details, a reference and the date it was verified. A **Declined by an agency** badge means an agency was given the lead and sent it back; it is in the pool again.

Below it, **Recent assignments** lists the last 20 leads given to agencies.

## How to use it

1. **Read the lead**: the business, category and message tell you what the visitor wants.
2. **Choose an agency** from the list. Each agency shows its active business types and active client count, so you can match the lead to an agency that serves that kind of business.
3. **Press Assign.** The agency is emailed and the lead leaves the pool. Only platform owners and staff see the Assign control; viewers read only.

## Common questions

### Why was I refused?

An agency that already holds the same visitor (same email) and business cannot be given the lead again. Pick another agency.

### Where do these leads come from?

From the platform's own request page. Leads from an agency's own intake link go to that agency, not to this pool.

### What happens to a lead nobody wants?

It stays in the pool. An agency can also send an assigned lead back, which marks it Declined by an agency and returns it here.

## What this page tells you

How {{product}} is doing across every agency, in five figures, three charts and a feed of recent events. It is for platform owners, staff and viewers.

The figures:

- **Agencies**: every agency on the platform.
- **Active clients**: clients with status active that are not paused.
- **Seats**: the people with an agency role plus the people with a client role.
- **Weekly active users**: people who used the app in the last 7 days, today included.
- **Spend this month**: AI and data cost recorded against an agency since the 1st of the month (UTC). Cost that is not tied to one agency is not in it; the Costs page covers the whole platform.

Each figure is today's live value. The small pill next to it, labelled **Last 28 days**, is the change since 28 days ago, taken from the daily figures stored then. There is no pill when nothing changed or nothing was recorded that day. For Spend this month the pill compares the month so far with the month-to-date total as it stood 28 days ago.

## How to use it

1. **Read the pills first.** A rising seat count with flat active clients, or a falling weekly active users figure, is where to look next.
2. **Switch the charts** between **12 weeks** (one point per week, weeks start on Monday) and **12 months** (one point per month). The toggle changes the charts only, not the figures above them. A gap in a line means nothing was recorded for that period.
3. **Scan Recent activity** for what just happened: an agency signing up, adding or activating a client, sending its first brief, becoming at risk, or having a support session opened. It shows 20 at a time; use **Show more** for older events.
4. **Click an agency name** in the feed to open its page.

## Common questions

### Why is a chart empty?

The charts are built from daily stored figures. A new environment shows "No history yet" until the first nightly run has written some.

### Why does Spend this month differ from the Costs page?

Overview counts only cost recorded against an agency. Costs shows what the vendors charge the platform in total, plus manual costs.

### What does at risk in the feed mean?

The agency's health flag turned to At risk. The rules are on the Agencies page.

## What this page tells you

Decisions the models could not settle with enough confidence, waiting for a person. Your answer fixes the event and is stored as a gold label.

Competitor changes (a new page, a price, a service) are classified by a cascade:

1. **Jev** answers first.
2. Any answer under **0.85 confidence** goes to a **language model**.
3. If that answer is also under 0.85, the question lands **here** for a **person**.

The same 0.85 threshold is the verifier's, the check that every brief claim is supported. Each decision task has its own threshold in the AI configuration; today they are all 0.85 except the Ask interpretation check.

Each card shows the competitor, the source and kind of change, and the text before and after. Under it are the questions the models were unsure about, each with **Model said:** the model's answer and its confidence.

## How to use it

1. **Read the before and after text.** Then answer each question in the list.
2. **Press Resolve.** The event is created, corrected or removed as your answers imply, and your answers are saved as gold labels. Nothing on this page changes the thresholds.
3. **Work oldest first.** The queue is ordered by age and shows 25 at a time, with Previous and Next links. Items whose change was superseded or suppressed are not listed.

## Common questions

### What does "Model said: No (20%)" mean?

The model's answer was No, with 20% confidence. Your answer replaces it.

### Should I change the threshold?

Not from this page. The project rule is to leave the verifier threshold at 0.85 until enough of these answers have been collected to measure it.

### Who can answer?

Any platform operator can; viewers included.

## What this page tells you

The standard runbook every agency starts from: plays (the recommendations a brief can suggest, each with a trigger, a title and a template), starting-point rules, and settings (alert and brief thresholds, focus services and competitor tiers). Each agency gets its own copy, and each client can in turn get a copy of the agency's.

Changing an item here does not rewrite an agency's copy. The agency's item shows **Update available**, and its admins choose to use the update or keep their own version. An item you add shows as **New** for them, and one you remove shows as **Removed upstream**.

Each item has a badge that compares it with its parent and an on/off switch. Platform owners and staff can edit; viewers can read. Nobody can edit in a read-only support session.

## How to use it

1. **Edit a play** to change its title or template. **Preview** shows how the template reads.
2. **Switch items off** that no agency should inherit by default.
3. **Add or remove items** to change what agencies are offered. Agencies decide whether to take each change.
4. **Remember the audience.** Agencies see these words in their own runbook, worded by their assistant.

## Common questions

### Does a change reach every agency at once?

It reaches each agency as an update that its admins choose to accept or decline. If the agency customised the item, the review shows both versions.

### Which clients use these plays directly?

Clients whose business type has no plays of its own and no runbook copy use the agency's runbook, which starts as a copy of this one. HVAC and dental clients keep their built-in plays until they get a runbook of their own.

### Why are the controls disabled?

You are a platform viewer, or you are in a read-only support session.

## What this page tells you

New review topics found in reviews that did not fit any existing topic, waiting for your decision.

A proposal appears like this: every night, for each business type, reviews that matched none of its topics are collected. When at least **20** of them from the last **90 days** have built up since the last proposal, a model reads a sample (up to 40) and looks for one specific, recurring topic that at least **a fifth** of them share. If it finds one, it proposes a topic name and a one-line description. A business type has one open proposal at a time. "N reviews with no topic" is how many reviews it looked at.

## How to use it

1. **Read the name, description and sample quotes.** Is it a real, recurring topic for that business type, and not already covered?
2. **Approve** to add it: it is asked for every new review in that business type, and reviews from the last **180 days** are checked for it too. **Reject** to turn it down: it is not proposed again.
3. **Check Recently decided** for the last 30 days of decisions.

## Common questions

### Does approving check older reviews?

Yes, back to 180 days. After you approve a topic, reviews of that business type from the last 180 days are checked for it in the background, after any new reviews and at most 2,000 reviews a day across the platform. Older reviews are not checked. Until the check is done, the topic's numbers are based on fewer reviews. The same check runs when a business type's topics are edited, and when a competitor starts being tracked for another business type.

### Can I undo a decision?

Not from this page. A proposal someone else already decided shows an error.

### Why is the list empty?

No business type has collected enough unmatched reviews yet, or one already has an open proposal.

The review queue for business types and services (business areas) that agencies created while setting up clients. The number on the menu item counts both lists.

- **New business types**: each card shows the name and id, who added it, how many clients use it, its Google categories and services, and an **Evidence** list of the quotes it was drafted from.
- **New services**: services added to an already reviewed business type, with their other names.

Platform owners and staff can act; viewers read the queue but see no buttons.

1. **Approve** a business type that is right. It is marked reviewed together with the services it came with. Approve a service on its own the same way.
2. **Rename** to fix a name. The id never changes. A name cannot include a client's business name, phone number, email or web address.
3. **Edit** (business types only) to change the keywords, Google categories, review topics and services before approving.
4. **Merge into** a duplicate. Everything of the duplicate moves to the entry you pick: its clients, events, prices and agency settings. The old id keeps resolving to the target. For a business type you also say where each of its services goes; matching names are pre-filled, and "Move" keeps a service as a new one. A service merges into another service of the same business type.

## Common questions

### What happens to the old business type?

Clients, events, prices and agency settings move to the target, and the old id keeps resolving to it.

### Why can't I see any buttons?

You are a platform viewer. Owners and staff can change the catalogue.

### Where do the quotes come from?

They are the evidence recorded when the business type was drafted, and show why each service was proposed.

## What this page tells you

People who joined the pilot waitlist from the public website. The page has three tabs, each with the number of new entries in brackets:

- **Agencies**: agencies that want to be invited. Each row shows the agency, the contact, the email address, how many clients it manages and its business type.
- **Businesses**: local businesses that want to be passed to an agency, with their business type and place.
- **Sample requests**: agencies that asked for a sample brief, with the business they named and how far the sample has got. ## How to use it

1. **Pick a tab** and read the new entries. The status chip tells you where each one stands: New, Invited, Assigned or Declined. A sample shows Requested, In progress, Sent, Declined or Stopped.
2. **Search** when you are looking for one person or business.

## Common questions

### Why can't I invite this agency?

Its email address is not confirmed yet, or it has already been invited. Only confirmed, new entries can be invited.

### Why is a sample request not counted?

Samples count only once the agency has confirmed its email address, and they use one of the month's sample briefs when you approve them, not when they arrive.

### Where does a sample go after I approve it?

The business is created in the Samples agency and its setup opens. Only the operator who approved the sample becomes a member of the Samples agency, so that operator finishes its setup; other operators approve their own samples. Run setup as usual, approve the starting point in Approvals, then send the sample from here.

### What should I do on the competitors step of a sample's setup?

Pick the rivals yourself. Do not use "Ask the owner to pick": a sample business has no owner, so the starting point would wait for the 14-day cap before it was built.

### What does Send again do?

**Send again** issues a fresh link and cancels the older sample links, so only the newest one opens.

### How long does a sample link work?

A sample link ends 30 days after it was sent. Send again if the agency needs more time.

# Reading your weekly brief

Each week {{product}} sends a competitor brief for your business. It is also available in your dashboard, and you can download it as a PDF from the email.

## The summary

The brief opens with a short summary. In a week with real changes it is headed **This week**. If nothing important happened, the heading is **A quiet week**, and the brief says so instead of padding it out.

## The numbered items

Each item is a card with a headline about one competitor. Every item has the same parts:

- **What changed**: what was seen, such as a new price, offer, page or review pattern.
- **Why it matters**: what the change could mean for your business. This part appears when there is a clear reason.
- **What to do**: a suggested next step. This also appears only when there is one.

A line at the bottom of the card names the competitor and gives a low, medium or high rating for the effort of acting and the likely impact.

Every item rests on evidence. Use the **See the evidence** link in the email, or the evidence in the dashboard, to check the original source.

## Trends

Some briefs include a small trend table comparing businesses over a recent window of days. Use it for context rather than as a verdict.

## Next steps

Use **Open in your dashboard** in the email to see the full brief and its evidence. To go deeper, ask {{assistant}} a question about any item, and save a useful answer as a recommendation.

Your agency has paused monitoring for your business. No new checks, briefs or alerts arrive until it is resumed.
For example, a business that holds 12 of 60 top-3 spots has a 20% share of voice. Businesses that are not tracked are grouped as "Other businesses".
Of all the top-3 map spots in a weekly rank scan (every grid point and search term), the share each business holds.
Rank scans read the first 20 map results from each point of a grid spread across the service area.
The few businesses Google shows with a map at the top of local search results. Here it means the top 3 map results.
A point where the business is not in the first 20 results counts as 21.
For one search term, the average position a business holds in Google Maps results across all points of the rank grid. 1 is best.
How fast a business gets new Google reviews, shown as reviews per month: the reviews posted in the last 6 months, divided by 6.

Tiers come from two checks. Overlap: how often the business shows up in Google Maps searches for the same services nearby (a higher spot, a shorter distance and the same main category count for more). Activity: its Google and Meta ads, its new reviews in the last 30 days and whether it has claimed its Google profile. A Top rival is high on both, Worth watching is high on either, and the rest are Minor. When activity could not be checked, Worth watching is the highest tier possible.
How closely a competitor competes: Top rival, Worth watching or Minor.
It shows a dash when there were no reviews in that time.
The share of a business's Google reviews from the last 90 days that have a reply from the owner.
A topic's share is the percentage of the reviews checked for that topic in the last 90 days that mention it. Its sentiment runs from very negative to very positive.
A topic customers bring up in reviews, such as response time, price transparency or cleanliness. Each business type has its own list.
It is prepared once the competitor list is set, from the Google profile, reviews, map rankings and competitors, and suggests first steps.
The first brief for a new business: where it stands against its competitors before weekly briefs begin.
Do not mix them up with a move, which is a pattern in a competitor's changes. The starting point lists the first steps that are still open.
The first actions suggested for your business in the starting point. They are your own to-dos, not something a competitor did.
Each one moves from To do to In progress to Done, or can be dismissed.
A suggested next step, from a brief or saved from a chat answer, with an effort and impact rating.
No evidence, no claim: nothing goes into a brief or an alert without it.
The proof behind a claim: a screenshot or the captured text, with where and when it was captured.

Reaching the limit changes nothing: monitoring, briefs and Ask carry on, and the client shows as Limit reached. If work runs well past the limit, AI and monitoring work for that client pauses until the 1st of next month, while past briefs and evidence stay available.
How this product counts the AI and data work done for a client each month. Each client has a monthly credit limit, and a calendar month in UTC is the period.
Only agency staff see it. It is removed from everything the client sees.
A note on a brief item or recommendation naming a service your agency could offer in response, such as local SEO, PPC or reputation work.
The same change seen in several places, say the website and an ad, is shown once. Every change links to its evidence and gets a score.
One difference found in a competitor's public information, such as a new price, a new offer or page, an ad that started or stopped, or a jump in reviews.

A move starts as Emerging. It becomes Active once it has held for 7 days, or straight away when the evidence is strong. It is Fading when no new supporting change has appeared for 30 days, and it closes when the pattern has not held for 30 days.
A pattern in one competitor's changes over the last 90 days, such as a price war, a promo blitz, an ad surge, a new service line or a push into new areas.

A highlighted pill is worth a look, for example 5 or more new reviews in 30 days, or Google ads that started in the last 30 days. "Not checked" means the fact could not be read yet; it never means zero.
A quick fact about a competitor, shown as a small pill: its Google rating, its new reviews in the last 30 days, its Google ads and its Meta ads.
A quiet week says so instead of padding the brief, and shows "Where you stand": how the business compares with its competitors on rating, new reviews, reply rate and map positions.
The weekly report on competitors, dated each Monday. Each item says what changed, why it matters and what to do, with its evidence.
A look at competitor trends over a whole quarter, as a page and a PDF. The first one arrives after a full quarter of monitoring.
A change important enough not to wait for the weekly brief: its score reached the alert level. Alerts arrive between briefs.

It combines the scores of its changes from the last 30 days that made the brief or an alert, plus its open moves (active, confident moves count for more). Each one adds to the total without it passing 100. 70 and above is High pressure, 40 to 69 is Medium pressure, 1 to 39 is Low pressure, and a competitor with nothing recent scores 0 and shows as Quiet.
How much a competitor has been doing lately that could affect the business, from 0 to 100.

Type: how much this kind of change usually matters. Size: how big it is, such as the size of a price cut. Relevance: whether it touches services the business offers and, for changes to a service area, the area it serves. Novelty: whether it is new rather than a repeat of something already seen. By default a score of 70 or more is an alert, 40 or more goes in the brief, and anything lower is archived.
How much a change matters to the business, from 0 to 100. It is 100 × type × size × relevance × novelty, each factor between 0 and 1.
